summary.text: A 61-year-old man with hypertension, stable angina and symptomatic Mobitz type 1 second-degree AV block, whose father died in his 50s of an unprovoked massive PE, presented to an urgent treatment centre with progressive left upper-limb swelling and pain five days after DDD pacemaker implantation (left axillary vein route).

Examination showed an erythematous, markedly swollen, tender left upper limb with dilated superficial veins over the left brachial area, warm left axilla, preserved radial/ulnar/brachial pulses (CRT 2 s), a 2 x 2 cm haematoma at the pacemaker site and a well-healed wound. NEWS was 0. Differentials were cellulitis, thrombophlebitis and DVT. Table 1 values included CRP 12.5 mg/L (reference <5) although the narrative calls inflammatory markers normal; chest X-ray showed satisfactory lead position without pneumothorax.

He received treatment-dose subcutaneous enoxaparin and next-day US compression venography (out-of-hours US unavailable) confirmed extensive occlusive axillary and subclavian thrombus with patent brachial and internal jugular veins. A previous echocardiogram two months earlier showed impaired LV function (LVEF 45-48%). No pacemaker checks were done.

He was transferred for cardiology review, which recommended three months of anticoagulation. Therapeutic enoxaparin continued in hospital and was switched to apixaban for a further three months at discharge, with aspirin withheld. Thrombophilia and malignancy screens were negative; PE was not investigated as there were no suggestive signs. DVT clinic follow-up at three months confirmed DVT resolution.

summary.text: An 84-year-old man with CALR-positive essential thrombocythaemia on hydroxycarbamide and aspirin, who had a DDD pacemaker implanted three months earlier for complete heart block, presented with a five-day history of progressive left upper-limb swelling with dilated superficial veins over the left chest wall and shoulder; he denied pain, shortness of breath and chest pain.

Examination showed a swollen left arm (33 cm vs 28 cm on the right) with pitting oedema to the mid-forearm, collateral superficial veins, left radial pulse present, CRT 3 s and warm peripheries; NEWS 0. Laboratory results included D-dimer >1000 ng/ml, WCC 3.6, Hb 126 g/L, platelets 331 and CRP <5. The differential included DVT, cellulitis, haematoma and thrombophlebitis.

US compression venography confirmed occlusive thrombus in the left subclavian and axillary veins with a patent left jugular vein. Haematology recommended CT TAP and tumour markers; tumour markers were negative and CT TAP confirmed the left subclavian thrombus with no definite malignancy. Previous echocardiogram three months earlier showed LVEF 65-70%; no pacemaker checks were done.

Therapeutic enoxaparin was started; interventional radiology advised that the clot was thrombosed with collateral flow so no acute intervention was needed, and vascular surgery recommended conservative anticoagulation. Enoxaparin was switched to rivaroxaban at discharge. The authors judged him at high risk of recurrent thrombosis and increased hydroxycarbamide. At haematology follow-up the next month his symptoms had notably improved.
